title: Design: contracts, breach and damages paid in operational budget
description: Operator ratified 2026-10-08 (decision 2): damages are measured in operational budget, never in reputation. Design, no code. Define 3 things: (a) CONTRACT, a commitment on an operational parameter the agent sets for itself (PR-060 clauses 1-2: task, order, budget, deadline, engine, iteration bound); (b) BREACH, a fact a verifier can replay, never a figure computed about an identity (PR-060 clause 5: doubt resolves toward constitutional); (c) DAMAGES, counted in tokens, tasks or deadline days. Answer each: whose budget pays; who receives it (the harmed party or nobody); a cap so repeated breach never turns into exclusion by computed standing (PR-026 clause 3); how each consequence gets its own published record naming the parameter, the consequence and the agent's own act of setting it (PR-060 clause 6); what keeps a false claim from being cheap; whether the non-staking rule (PR-061 clause 3, D-17) reaches budget or only reputation. Reputation is untouched: PR-022 clause 4, PR-026 and PR-061 stay intact. Who signed a contract inherits the D-17 limit; state it, do not solve it. The suits register and the judge are decision 3, still pending: name the interface, do not design the court. Input: the Swiss debt-enforcement research brief the coordinator attaches at dispatch. Output: .harness/design-T-436-contracts.md. Do not touch trust/, constitutional/ or keys/. The operator approves the design before any worker task is created.
acceptance_criteria: A design document exists at .harness/design-T-436-contracts.md and defines contract, breach and damages in 1 paragraph each.
Damages are counted only in tokens, tasks or deadline days; the document names no path by which reputation moves.
Each of the 6 questions in the description has a written answer or is marked open with the reason.
Every cited clause (PR-060 c1, c2, c5, c6; PR-022 c4; PR-026 c3; PR-061 c3) is quoted from the record, not paraphrased from memory.
No file under .harness/trust, .harness/constitutional or .harness/keys is read or written.
Handed off to a verifier; not self-marked done.

Replayed all 4 attacks plus clause checks myself (not copied from the thinker note):

(1) identity-figure damage: no success. Every damage path in section 3 (token/deadline/iteration
debit) and section 5 (false-claim debit) is computed from a single task's own committed-vs-observed
gap, never aggregated across tasks or by name; no stored balance field is created (matches PR-060
validity_conditions item 3). Holds.

(2) PR-026 c3 exclusion-by-standing: no success as a *constitutional* violation -- the design keeps
no running per-name count, so there is no "computed standing" figure for PR-026 c3 to bite on. Real
non-blocking weakness found and already partially covered by the design's own disclosure: nothing
caps a single severe breach's debit against the *size of the next task's own allocation*, so one
large gap could zero or exceed a future task's budget. Section 6 already flags "the exact numeric
schedule...is not fixed here...leaves the numbers for the operator to ratify," which covers this,
but the design should be explicit that the floor/ceiling on the debit-vs-next-task-allocation ratio
is one of those numbers, to block a de facto (if not formally "standing"-based) starvation path.

(3) consequence with no record of its own: no success. Section 4's generic "Each consequence's
published record is the only thing that attaches it" plausibly covers the section 5 false-claim
billing and the dependent-task priority bump; section 6 already flags the priority-bump schema as
open. Holds, with the caveat that section 5 never explicitly cross-references section 4 for its own
billing -- worth tightening in a revision but not a standalone failure.

(4) SUCCEEDS -- cheap claim as weapon. Design section 5, quoted exactly from
.harness/design-T-436-contracts.md: "A false claim therefore costs the claimant operational budget,
in the identical currency a real breach would have cost the respondent, rather than being void and
free," and earlier: "that non-replay is itself a breach of the claimant's own filing commitment,
billed in the same unit, against the same next-claimable-task budget, and bounded by the same cap as
section 3." Section 3's cap is defined as "bounded to the gap between the committed value and the
observed value for that one task." For a FALSE claim, by definition the real observed value shows no
breach, so the real gap for the respondent's task is zero -- the cap formula as written prices the
penalty off a real quantity that does not exist in the false-claim case. The document never states
whether the penalty is instead sized off the CLAIMANT's own alleged (false) gap; if it is, the
claimant can allege an arbitrarily small shortfall and pay an arbitrarily small penalty while still
filing a permanent, public, immutable record (section 4) naming the innocent respondent's commit act
next to an accusation -- and unlike attest.py's own DIS-4 for the structurally analogous fork/contest
case ("A CONTESTED ACT CARRIES NO WEIGHT UNTIL ADJUDICATED, INCLUDING THE FORGER'S"), this document
never states that a dismissed/false claim carries no evidentiary weight or cannot be cited later.
Section 5's own closing assurance -- "It cannot be used as a weapon for the same structural reasons
section 3 gives" -- only rebuts repeat-filing accrual and ambiguous-replay-favors-respondent; it does
not rebut this single-cheap-claim-plus-permanent-record vector, so the invulnerability claim is
overstated as written.

Section 3 and section 6 gained the non-blocking fix the verifier also flagged: an explicit second, independent cap -- a debit is bounded both to its own task's gap AND to a floor/ceiling ratio against the size of the NEXT task's own allocation it is charged to, so one severe breach cannot zero out an unrelated future task; the exact ratio is left, with the other numbers, for the operator to ratify. (2) PR-026 c3 exclusion by computed standing: no success, and round 1's non-blocking starvation caveat is now closed. Section 3 adds the promised second cap: "the debit is also capped against the size of the next task's own allocation it is charged to (a floor/ceiling ratio...)", carried into section 5's false-claim billing ("further bounded by section 3's next-task-allocation ceiling") and listed in section 6's open-numbers list. (3) consequence with no record of its own: no success, and round 1's caveat is closed. Section 4 now states explicitly: "This is the one record format for every consequence this design names... Section 5's billing is not a second record type; it cross-references this section." Section 5's own "Published record" paragraph cross-references section 4 rather than restating it. Holds.

(4) SUCCEEDS AGAIN, via target selection instead of alleged-value. Round 2 fixed the round-1 lever (claimant could not set the price by alleging a small gap): section 5 now prices a dismissed claim at "the FULL committed value of the operational parameter it named ... exactly as recorded in the respondent's own section 1 commit act -- never a fraction, and never a number the claimant supplies." That closes alleged-value manipulation. But the claimant still chooses WHICH of the respondent's commit acts to name in the claim -- the design never restricts a claim to the respondent's largest, or any particular, commitment. A claimant wanting a cheap weapon simply targets the respondent's smallest-committed-value task (e.g. a 1-iteration-bound commit, or a minimal token budget on a trivial task) and files a false claim against it: the price is "the full committed value of the parameter it named," which is small because the TARGET is small, not because the allegation is small. The claimant still gets a permanent, public record (section 4's format) naming the innocent respondent next to an accusation, at a cost the claimant chose by choosing the target -- the exact Schikanebetreibung pattern the Swiss brief warns against (sec 8 item 5, sec 3: "false claims are void but nearly free... deterrence against false claims is weak"), just routed around the specific fix round 2 made. Section 5's own closing defense -- "the price is fixed at the full committed value of the parameter the claim names, independent of whatever the claimant alleges" -- is true but non-responsive to this: it rebuts control over the ALLEGED VALUE, not control over the TARGET. No part of section 3, 5 or 6 states a price floor independent of the named parameter's own committed value, and no part of section 6's "left unsettled" list flags target-selection as an open risk. The document's invulnerability claim ("It cannot be used as a weapon for the same structural reasons section 3 gives") is therefore still overstated as written, for a different reason than round 1's.

Design section 5, quoted exactly from .harness/design-T-436-contracts.md, Outcome A: "the
filing is REFUSED, and no record naming the respondent is ever published... it attaches to
no respondent and names no accusation anywhere a future decision could read. The only trace
is the filing act itself, sitting -- exactly as DIS-5 already states for a forgery claim --
permanently on the CLAIMANT's own chain, never the respondent's."

This is factually wrong about the mechanism the design itself adopts. Section 5 explicitly
models filing on the EXISTING, already-built attest.py contest: "A claim is filed the same
way attest.py contest already files a forgery claim: a signed act on the CLAIMANT's own
chain, naming the respondent's commit act, the parameter it set, and the independent
observed source." I read .harness/bin/attest.py's actual contest()/sign_act() code (not the
design's gloss of it):

  def contest(root, accuser, key_path, target_name, target_seq, reason, task=None):
      ...
      return sign_act(root, accuser, key_path, "contest",
                      ref=f"{target_name}#{target_seq}", task=task,
                      body={"reason": reason, "AF_3": ..., "AF_4": ...})

and inside sign_act(), the act dict that gets written to a permanent plaintext JSON file is:

  act = {..., "kind": kind, "ref": ref, "body": body if body is not None else {}, ...}
  with os.fdopen(fd, "w", ...) as fh:
      fh.write(json.dumps(act, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

So the filing act's `ref` field is LITERALLY `{respondent_name}#{respondent_seq}` -- the
respondent's own commit-act identifier -- and `body.reason` carries the accusation text,
both written permanently to a plaintext file any agent on this shared-filesystem machine can
`cat` (D-17: "every agent runs as the same OS user on one filesystem"), independent of
whether any CLI's terse renderer (`chain`'s own printer only shows seq/kind/prev/signed, not
ref/body) chooses to display it. That directly contradicts "no record naming the respondent
is ever published," "it attaches to no respondent," and "names no accusation anywhere a
future decision could read" -- the record names the respondent and the accusation by
construction, and is "a future decision could read" it because nothing stops a read, only a
design-document instruction (the non-citability paragraph) not yet enforced by any tool.

This is exactly the weapon Swiss brief section 8 item 5 and section 3 warn about
(Schikanebetreibung: "false claims are void but nearly free... the target is not
automatically compensated" -- verbatim, docs/precedent-research/21-swiss-identity-and-
enforcement.md lines 39/86) -- a claimant files, pays nothing (section 5's own text: "a
refused filing costs nothing beyond the act itself"), gets refused, yet a permanent,
plaintext, respondent-naming accusation record exists forever and is trivially readable by
anyone with filesystem access, including a human operator skimming .harness/attest/ before
any "non-citability" policy could be mechanically enforced (no such enforcement exists in
code; it is asserted only in this design document). The design's "it attaches to no
respondent" is true only in the narrow PR-060 clause-2/clause-6 sense (no operational
parameter is debited), not in the plain-English sense the passage's own wording ("no record
naming the respondent," "no accusation anywhere... could read") claims.

Note: this finding does NOT require forging anything (the observed artifact, the commit act,
or the signature) -- it is a plain reading of the UNFORGED, honestly-filed REFUSED claim's
own on-disk shape -- so per the dispatch's own rule this is a genuine attack-4 success, not
the D-17 residual routed in section 6.

kind="contest" once the gap is confirmed. A REFUSED claim (no gap) therefore writes
